claim: The inner layer of blood vessels consists of endothelial cells, which form the physical barrier between blood and tissue.
source: The inner layer of blood vessels consists of endothelial cells, which form the physical barrier between blood and tissue.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about vascular anatomy and endothelial cell function.

claim: The vascular barrier is tightly regulated and is defined by cell-cell contacts through adherens and tight junctions.
source: This vascular barrier is tightly regulated and is defined by cell-cell contacts through adherens and tight junctions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vascular barrier structure and regulation.

claim: Rho GTPases are regulators of the actin cytoskeleton and are known to control junction integrity.
source: To investigate the signaling that regulates vascular barrier strength, we focused on Rho GTPases, regulators of the actin cytoskeleton and known to control junction integrity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rho GTPase function, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Guanine-nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) domains from ITSN1, TIAM1, and p63RhoGEF activate Cdc42, Rac, and Rho, respectively.
source: Guanine-nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) domains from ITSN1, TIAM1, and p63RhoGEF, activating Cdc42, Rac, and Rho, respectively, were integrated into the optogenetic recruitment tool improved light-induced dimer (iLID).
evidence: This is supported by citations in the methods and results sections describing the specificity of these GEF domains.

claim: The iLID tool allows for Rho GTPase activation at the subcellular level in a reversible and non-invasive manner.
source: This tool allows for Rho GTPase activation at the subcellular level in a reversible and non-invasive manner by recruiting a GEF to a specific area at the plasma membrane
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing local and global activation with reversibility.

claim: The membrane tag of iLID was optimized and a HaloTag was applied to gain more flexibility for multiplex imaging.
source: The membrane tag of iLID was optimized and a HaloTag was applied to gain more flexibility for multiplex imaging.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing CaaX and Lck membrane tags and the use of HaloTag with different fluorophores.

claim: Opto-RhoGEFs demonstrated precise temporal control of vascular barrier strength in an endothelial cell monolayer.
source: The resulting optogenetically recruitable RhoGEFs (Opto-RhoGEFs) were tested in an endothelial cell monolayer and demonstrated precise temporal control of vascular barrier strength by a cell-cell overlap-dependent, VE-cadherin-independent, mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements showing rapid and reversible changes in barrier strength.

claim: Opto-RhoGEFs control vascular barrier strength by a cell-cell overlap-dependent, VE-cadherin-independent mechanism.
source: The resulting optogenetically recruitable RhoGEFs (Opto-RhoGEFs) were tested in an endothelial cell monolayer and demonstrated precise temporal control of vascular barrier strength by a cell-cell overlap-dependent, VE-cadherin-independent, mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using VE-cadherin blocking antibody and microscopy observations of cell-cell overlap.

claim: Opto-RhoGEFs enabled precise optogenetic control in endothelial cells over morphological features such as cell size, cell roundness, local extension, and cell contraction.
source: Furthermore, Opto-RhoGEFs enabled precise optogenetic control in endothelial cells over morphological features such as cell size, cell roundness, local extension, and cell contraction.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing changes in cell area, form factor, and local protrusions upon photo-activation.

claim: Membrane protrusions at the junction region can rapidly increase barrier integrity independent of VE-cadherin.
source: In conclusion, we have optimized and applied the optogenetic iLID GEF recruitment tool, that is Opto-RhoGEFs, to study the role of Rho GTPases in the vascular barrier of the endothelium and found that membrane protrusions at the junction region can rapidly increase barrier integrity independent of VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing barrier strength increase in the presence of VE-cadherin blocking antibody and microscopy observations.

claim: The endothelium functions as a physical barrier between tissue and blood.
source: The endothelium lines the inner layer of blood vessels and functions as a physical barrier between tissue and blood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about endothelial function.

claim: The endothelial barrier is permeable for gases, nutrients, ions, water, and leukocytes.
source: However, this barrier is permeable for gases, nutrients, ions, water, and also leukocytes, with which every organ in the human body is maintained.
evidence: This is established knowledge about endothelial permeability.

claim: Dysregulation of endothelial barrier processes is linked to pathologies such as edema, arthritis, chronic inflammation, chronic bowel disease, cancer, and infections.
source: The dysregulation of these processes is linked to pathologies such as edema, arthritis, chronic inflammation, chronic bowel disease, cancer, infections, and other conditions (Claesson-Welsh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Claesson-Welsh et al., 2021.

claim: Adherens junctions are stable anchor points where endothelial cells attach to each other.
source: Two types of junctions are especially important in the endothelium, namely adherens junctions, which are stable anchor points where cells attach to each other, and tight junctions, which seal off the two cell edges tightly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about junction types and their functions.

claim: Tight junctions seal off the two cell edges tightly.
source: Two types of junctions are especially important in the endothelium, namely adherens junctions, which are stable anchor points where cells attach to each other, and tight junctions, which seal off the two cell edges tightly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about junction types and their functions.

claim: Transport of ions and small molecules below 800 Da happens via tight junctions.
source: Regarding permeability, the transport of ions and small molecules below 800 Da happens via the tight junctions; transport of larger molecules and leukocytes across the endothelium is regulated by adherens junctions (Duong and Vestweber, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duong and Vestweber, 2020.

claim: Transport of larger molecules and leukocytes across the endothelium is regulated by adherens junctions.
source: Regarding permeability, the transport of ions and small molecules below 800 Da happens via the tight junctions; transport of larger molecules and leukocytes across the endothelium is regulated by adherens junctions (Duong and Vestweber, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duong and Vestweber, 2020.

claim: Linear adherens junctions show low leakage and are referred to as mature or stable adherens junctions.
source: Typically, linear adherens junctions show low leakage and are referred to as mature or stable adherens junctions (Angulo-Urarte et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Angulo-Urarte et al., 2020.

claim: Homotypic VE-cadherin intercellular bonds are believed to mainly contribute to vascular barrier strength.
source: Homotypic VE-cadherin intercellular bonds are believed to mainly contribute to the vascular barrier strength (Breviario et al., 1995; Gotsch et al., 1997; van Buul et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Breviario et al., 1995; Gotsch et al., 1997; van Buul et al., 2002.

claim: VE-cadherins bind homotypically to the VE-cadherin of the neighboring cell.
source: VE-cadherins are the typical vascular cadherins that bind homotypically to the VE-cadherin of the neighboring cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VE-cadherin function.

claim: VE-cadherins exist in a protein complex including p120, alpha, beta and gamma catenin that eventually connects to the actin network via α-catenin.
source: They exist in a protein complex, including p120, alpha, beta and gamma catenin and this complex eventually connects to the actin network via α-catenin (Angulo-Urarte et al., 2020; Dejana, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Angulo-Urarte et al., 2020; Dejana, 2004.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton defines cell morphology and influences the organization of junctions.
source: The actin cytoskeleton does not only define the cell morphology but also influences the organization of junctions (Yamamoto et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yamamoto et al., 2021.

claim: Increased permeability and reduced vascular barrier strength is associated with altered junction organization and gap formation.
source: Increased permeability and thereby reduced vascular barrier strength is associated with altered junction organization and gap formation (Claesson-Welsh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Claesson-Welsh et al., 2021.

claim: Permeability is regulated by phosphorylation of junction proteins.
source: On a molecular level, permeability is regulated by phosphorylation of junction proteins (Claesson-Welsh et al., 2021; Vestweber, 2021), which induce reorganization of the junctions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Claesson-Welsh et al., 2021; Vestweber, 2021.

claim: Phosphorylation of junction proteins is initiated by signaling molecules such as histamine, bradykinin, S1P, which are ligands for GPCRs expressed in the endothelium.
source: This phosphorylation is initiated by signaling molecules such as histamine, bradykinin, S1P, which are ligands for the GPCRs expressed in the endothelium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR signaling in endothelial cells.

claim: GPCR-induced signaling cascades often involve Rho GTPases, which regulate the actin cytoskeleton and junction organization.
source: The GPCR-induced signaling cascades often involve Rho GTPases, which among others regulate the actin cytoskeleton and thereby junction organization as well.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR and Rho GTPase signaling.

claim: Rho GTPases are molecular switches that are 'ON' when bound to GTP and 'OFF' when bound to GDP.
source: Rho GTPases are molecular switches that are 'ON' when they are bound to GTP and 'OFF' when they are bound to GDP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rho GTPase function.

claim: In the 'ON' state, Rho GTPases initiate their signaling cascade, which leads to remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: In the 'ON' state they initiate their signaling cascade, which among other options leads to the remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rho GTPase signaling.

claim: Rho guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) facilitate the exchange of GDP to GTP, thereby turning Rho GTPases on.
source: Rho GTPases are in turn regulated by Rho guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), which facilitate the exchange of GDP to GTP, thereby they turn the Rho GTPase on.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GEF function.

claim: G-protein activating proteins enhance the intrinsic Rho GTPase hydrolysis function to hydrolyze GTP to GDP and switch them off.
source: In contrast, G-protein activating proteins enhance the intrinsic Rho GTPase hydrolysis function to hydrolyze GTP to GDP and they thereby switch off.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GAP function.

claim: Active Rho GTPases are typically located at the plasma membrane.
source: Active Rho GTPases are typically located at the plasma membrane, inactive once can be bound by GDP dissociation inhibitors and localize in the cytosol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rho GTPase localization.

claim: Inactive Rho GTPases can be bound by GDP dissociation inhibitors and localize in the cytosol.
source: Active Rho GTPases are typically located at the plasma membrane, inactive once can be bound by GDP dissociation inhibitors and localize in the cytosol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rho GTPase localization.

claim: Rho activity is associated with cell contraction and actin stress fiber formation localized at rear edge of a migrating cell.
source: Rho activity is associated with cell contraction and actin stress fiber formation localized at rear edge of a migrating cell and decreased vascular barrier strength, for example, induced by histamine and thrombin (Beckers et al., 2010; Hall, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beckers et al., 2010; Hall, 1998.

claim: Rho activity is associated with decreased vascular barrier strength, for example, induced by histamine and thrombin.
source: Rho activity is associated with cell contraction and actin stress fiber formation localized at rear edge of a migrating cell and decreased vascular barrier strength, for example, induced by histamine and thrombin (Beckers et al., 2010; Hall, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beckers et al., 2010; Hall, 1998.

claim: Rac1 activity is associated with lamellipodia formation and cell spreading.
source: Rac1 activity is associated with lamellipodia formation and cell spreading, and Cdc42 activity with formation of filopodia both Rac1 and Cdc42 localizing at leading edge of a migrating cell and promote increased vascular barrier strength, for example, by the stimulation with S1P (Hall, 1998; Reinhard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall, 1998; Reinhard et al., 2017.

claim: Cdc42 activity is associated with formation of filopodia.
source: Rac1 activity is associated with lamellipodia formation and cell spreading, and Cdc42 activity with formation of filopodia both Rac1 and Cdc42 localizing at leading edge of a migrating cell and promote increased vascular barrier strength, for example, by the stimulation with S1P (Hall, 1998; Reinhard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall, 1998; Reinhard et al., 2017.

claim: Rac1 and Cdc42 localize at leading edge of a migrating cell and promote increased vascular barrier strength.
source: Rac1 activity is associated with lamellipodia formation and cell spreading, and Cdc42 activity with formation of filopodia both Rac1 and Cdc42 localizing at leading edge of a migrating cell and promote increased vascular barrier strength, for example, by the stimulation with S1P (Hall, 1998; Reinhard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall, 1998; Reinhard et al., 2017.

claim: The activity of Rho GTPases is well defined in time and space, as shown by the polarization of migrating cells.
source: The polarization of the migrating cell shows that the activity of Rho GTPases is well defined in time and space (Welch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Welch et al., 2011.

claim: Local Rho activity is present at the cleavage furrow of a dividing cell coordinating a ring of contracting actin, limited in time to the duration of cell division.
source: To further illustrate there is local Rho activity present at the cleavage furrow of a dividing cell coordinating a ring of contracting actin, limited in time to the duration of cell division (Mahlandt et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mahlandt et al., 2021.

claim: Local Rho activity was observed at the migration pore in the endothelium during leukocyte transmigration, probably restricting the pore size with an actin ring.
source: local Rho activity was observed at the migration pore in the endothelium during leukocyte transmigration, probably restricting the pore size with an actin ring, limited in time to the duration of transmigration (Heemskerk et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heemskerk et al., 2016.

claim: Local Rac activity was observed in dorsal cell membrane ruffle.
source: local Rac activity was observed in dorsal cell membrane ruffle (Arts et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arts et al., 2021.

claim: Rho and Cdc42 waves were observed in Xenopus oocytes showing local patterns that move quickly over time.
source: Additionally, Rho and Cdc42 waves were observed in Xenopus oocytes showing incredible local patterns that move quickly over time (Moe et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moe et al., 2021.

claim: Rho GTPase signaling can occur in a global manner, for example during invagination in Drosophila embryo.
source: However, Rho GTPase signaling can also occur in a global manner, for example during invagination in Drosophila embryo (Izquierdo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Izquierdo et al., 2018.

claim: The rapamycin heterodimerization system utilizes GEF catalytic active DHPH domains by recruiting them to the plasma membrane.
source: Another method is the rapamycin heterodimerization system. This system utilizes the GEF catalytic active DHPH domains, by recruiting them to the plasma membrane, the natural location of Rho GTPases, where GDP for GTP exchange takes place.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the rapamycin system and is supported by citations.

claim: The rapamycin system requires two proteins that have low binding affinity in the absence of rapamycin and high binding affinity in its presence.
source: This method requires two proteins that have low binding affinity in the absence of rapamycin and high binding affinity in its presence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the rapamycin heterodimerization system.

claim: Rapamycin is involved in the mTOR pathway and may affect this pathway upon exogenous addition.
source: However, it needs to be stressed that rapamycin is not without side effects in a human cell, but in fact is involved in the mTOR pathway and hence may affect this pathway as well, upon exogenous addition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rapamycin's effects on cellular pathways.

claim: iLID and PhyB/PiF have been shown to trigger Rho GTPase activity and induce cell extension by optogenetic recruitment of TIAM-1 and ITSN.
source: For iLID and PhyB/PiF, it has been shown that the optogenetic recruitment of TIAM-1 and ITSN can be used to trigger Rho GTPase activity and thereby induce cell extension (Guntas et al., 2015; Levskaya et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guntas et al., 2015; Levskaya et al., 2009.

claim: BcLOV has been used to manipulate Rho GTPase activity.
source: Also BcLOV has been used to manipulate Rho GTPase activity (Berlew et al., 2022) as well as CRY2/CIB1 (Izquierdo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berlew et al., 2022 and Izquierdo et al., 2018.

claim: CRY2/CIB1 has been used to manipulate Rho GTPase activity.
source: Also BcLOV has been used to manipulate Rho GTPase activity (Berlew et al., 2022) as well as CRY2/CIB1 (Izquierdo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Izquierdo et al., 2018.

claim: iLID and enhanced Magnets (eMags) can be activated locally and globally, are fast inducible and reversible, relatively small in size, do not require co-factor addition to the cell medium, and can be targeted to a cellular structure of choice.
source: For this study, iLID and enhanced Magnets (eMags)-based optogenetic tools were chosen because they can be activated locally and globally, are fast inducible and reversible, relatively small in size, which is of advantage for lentiviral packing, do not require co-factor addition to the cell medium, and can be targeted to a cellular structure of choice.
evidence: This is based on the properties of these optogenetic tools as described in the literature.

claim: eMags showed the shortest t½ ON kinetics with 3.97 s and the fastest t½ OFF kinetics with 18.6 s.
source: eMags showed the shortest t½ ON kinetics with 3.97 s and the fastest t½ OFF kinetics with 18.6 s.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kinetics measurements shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: eMags had the lowest mean recruitment efficiency with a normalized membrane to cytosol intensity ratio of 1.5.
source: However, the mean efficiency of the recruitment measured by normalized membrane to cytosol intensity ratio was with 1.5 the lowest.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recruitment efficiency measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The iLID system showed comparable t½ ON kinetics of 5.14 s and t½ OFF kinetics of 20.3 s and had a higher mean recruitment efficiency than eMags.
source: The iLID system showed comparable t½ ON kinetics of 5.14 s and t½ OFF kinetics of 20.3 s and it had a higher mean recruitment efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kinetics and recruitment efficiency measurements shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The rapamycin system showed a longer t½ ON kinetics of 43.1 s.
source: The rapamycin system showed a longer t½ ON kinetics of 43.1 s, which may partly be explained by the different type of activation, as the rapamycin was added to the medium and needed to diffuse into the cell.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kinetics measurements shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The rapamycin system showed the highest recruitment efficiency with a normalized membrane to cytosol intensity ratio above 3.
source: The rapamycin system showed the highest recruitment efficiency with a normalized membrane to cytosol intensity ratio above 3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recruitment efficiency measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The rapamycin system showed the highest sensor localization at the plasma membrane with a median of 14% change in the membrane to cytosol intensity ratio for the PIP3 biosensor.
source: The rapamycin system showed the highest sensor localization at the plasma membrane with a median of 14% change in the membrane to cytosol intensity ratio and iLID showed a median change of 6.4%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from PIP3 biosensor measurements shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: iLID showed a median change of 6.4% in the membrane to cytosol intensity ratio for the PIP3 biosensor.
source: The rapamycin system showed the highest sensor localization at the plasma membrane with a median of 14% change in the membrane to cytosol intensity ratio and iLID showed a median change of 6.4%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from PIP3 biosensor measurements shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Activation of eMags showed no change in the intensity of the PI(3,4,5)P3 biosensor.
source: Unexpectedly, activation of eMags showed no change in the intensity of the PI(3,4,5)P3 biosensor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from PIP3 biosensor measurements shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: iLID tagged to the plasma membrane with Lck showed a higher median change in cytosolic intensity with 36.7% compared to CaaX-tagged iLID with 25.5%.
source: iLID tagged to the plasma membrane with Lck showed at higher median change in cytosolic intensity with 36.7%. The mean change in cytosolic intensity for the CaaX-tagged iLID was 25.5%; also its variance was larger compared to the Lck tag.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing membrane tags shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Rho sensor HaloTag-3xrGBD showed a clear relocation to the plasma membrane upon photo-activation of OptoP63.
source: The Rho sensor HaloTag-3xrGBD showed a clear relocation to the plasma membrane upon photo-activation of OptoP63, measured by fluorescent intensity decrease in the cytosol (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from biosensor measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The Cdc42 sensor dimericTomato-wGBD showed relocation to the plasma membrane upon photo-activation of OptoITSN.
source: The Cdc42 sensor dimericTomato-wGBD showed relocation to the plasma membrane upon photo-activation of OptoITSN (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from biosensor measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: OptoTIAM-expressing cells showed an increase in resistance after 1 min of activation with blue light, which is fully reversible within seconds.
source: OptoTIAM-expressing cells showed an increase in resistance after 1 min of activation with blue light, which is fully reversible within seconds.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When activating OptoTIAM for 10 min, the increase in resistance reached a maximum level.
source: When activating for 10 min, the increase in resistance reached a maximum level.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: During sequential activation of 15 min performed three times, OptoTIAM cells did not show any fatigue.
source: To study fatigue a sequential activation of 15 min was performed three times. Interestingly, during this period, the cellular system did not show any fatigue.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When OptoTIAM endothelial cells were activated for 2 hr, the maximum resistance level did not show any drop, but as soon as photo-activation was stopped, the resistance decreased drastically within seconds.
source: Even when the endothelial cells were activated for 2 hr, the maximum resistance level did not show any drop, but as soon as photo-activation was stopped, the resistance decreased drastically within seconds.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Control cells, only expressing the iLID part of the system, did not respond to the blue light with a change in resistance.
source: The control cells, only expressing the iLID part of the system, did not respond to the blue light with a change in resistance (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The resistance of OptoITSN-expressing endothelial cells showed a similar pattern to OptoTIAM cells but with a smaller amplitude.
source: The resistance of the OptoITSN-expressing endothelial cells showed a similar pattern in comparison to the OptoTIAM cells but with a smaller amplitude, indicating that Cdc42 activation did not increase endothelial resistance to the same extent as Rac did.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OptoITSN monolayer reached maximum resistance at approximately 5 min.
source: However, this monolayer reached maximum resistance at approximately 5 min.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When OptoITSN cells were photo-activated for longer than 10 min the resistance started to decrease slightly but did not return to baseline.
source: When OptoITSN cells were photo-activated for longer than 10 min the resistance started to decrease slightly but did not return to baseline.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OptoP63 cells showed a dip in resistance when activated for 1 min.
source: OptoP63 cells showed a dip in resistance when activated for 1 min.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When OptoP63 cells are activated for longer than 10 min, the resistance started to recover to baseline, even though the cells were still photo-activated.
source: When activated for longer than 10 min, the resistance started to recover to baseline, even so the cells were still photo-activated.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When OptoP63 cells are activated for 2 hr, the initial drop in resistance recovers to a value above the baseline level before the activation.
source: When the OptoP63 cells are activated for 2 hr, the initial drop in resistance recovers to a value above the baseline level before the activation.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: For OptoTIAM cells, increased cell-cell overlap was observed during photo-activation.
source: For some OptoTIAM cells, increased cell-cell overlap was observed during photo-activation.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2C and related animations.

claim: Some OptoITSN cells showed increased overlap and appeared to ruffle more during photo-activation.
source: Some OptoITSN cells also showed increased overlap and appeared to ruffle more during photo-activation.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2C and related animations.

claim: OptoP63 cells clearly showed contraction, as judged by the induction of gaps appearing in the monolayer upon photo-activation.
source: OptoP63 cells clearly showed contraction, as was judged by the induction of gaps appearing in the monolayer upon photo-activation.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2C and related animations.

claim: For OptoP63 cells, the formation of gaps between cells caused by cell contraction and partly loss of cell-cell junctions explains the decrease in resistance and barrier strength.
source: For the OptoP63 cells, the formation of gaps between cells caused by cell contraction and partly loss of cell-cell junctions explains the decrease in resistance and, accordingly, barrier strength.
evidence: This is inferred from microscopy observations and ECIS measurements.

claim: Comparing the junction linearity prior to activation and at the maximum of activation for OptoTIAM, the linearity index increased slightly.
source: Comparing the junction linearity prior to activation and at the maximum of activation for OptoTIAM, the linearity index increased slightly, for OptoITSN there was no change and for OptoP63 there was a slight increase in linearity index (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by linearity index measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For OptoITSN there was no change in linearity index comparing pre-activation and maximum activation.
source: Comparing the junction linearity prior to activation and at the maximum of activation for OptoTIAM, the linearity index increased slightly, for OptoITSN there was no change and for OptoP63 there was a slight increase in linearity index (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by linearity index measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For OptoP63 there was a slight increase in linearity index comparing pre-activation and maximum activation.
source: Comparing the junction linearity prior to activation and at the maximum of activation for OptoTIAM, the linearity index increased slightly, for OptoITSN there was no change and for OptoP63 there was a slight increase in linearity index (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by linearity index measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The VE-cadherin blocking antibody lowered the resistance in all conditions, which dropped to a stable level.
source: The VE-cadherin blocking antibody lowered the resistance in all conditions, which dropped to a stable level (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: After VE-cadherin blocking antibody treatment, OptoTIAM and OptoITSN cells were photo-activated and showed an increase in resistance comparable to the control conditions without the VE-cadherin blocking antibody.
source: Subsequently, the cells were photo-activated and for OptoTIAM and OptoITSN, an increase in resistance was measured comparable to the control conditions without the VE-cadherin blocking antibody.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: OptoP63 showed a decrease in resistance after VE-cadherin blocking antibody treatment, but the drop is not more severe in the presence of VE-cadherin blocking antibody.
source: OptoP63 showed a decrease in resistance, but the drop is not more severe in the presence of VE-cadherin blocking antibody.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Under conditions where blocking of VE-cadherin reduced the resistance of endothelial monolayers, the barrier could still be enhanced by photo-activating specific GEFs that activate Rho GTPases Rac1 or Cdc42.
source: Under conditions where blocking of VE-cadherin reduced the resistance of endothelial monolayers, the barrier could still be enhanced, independent from VE-cadherin. By photo-activating specific GEFs that subsequently activate Rho GTPases Rac1 or Cdc42, the endothelial barrier function can be increased.
evidence: This is supported by ECIS resistance measurements with VE-cadherin blocking antibody shown in Figure 3B.

claim: OptoTIAM and OptoITSN cells spread out in all directions upon activation and appeared rounder.
source: OptoTIAM and OptoITSN cells spread out in all directions upon activation. Therefore, these cells appeared rounder.
evidence: This is supported by cell area change measurements and form factor analysis shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: OptoP63 cells contracted and were less round upon activation.
source: In contrast, OptoP63 cells contracted and were less round (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cell area change measurements and form factor analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cells expressing OptoTIAM increased about 15% in size and reached the maximum at 10 min photo-activation.
source: Cells expressing OptoTIAM increased about 15% in size and reached the maximum at 10 min photo-activation.
evidence: This is supported by cell area measurements over time shown in Figure 4B.

claim: OptoITSN expressing cells reached the cell area maximum of 10% after roughly 3 min and after that the cell area slightly decreased during the photo-activation.
source: In comparison, OptoITSN expressing cells reached the cell area maximum of 10% after roughly 3 min and after that the cell area slightly decreased during the photo-activation.
evidence: This is supported by cell area measurements over time shown in Figure 4B.

claim: OptoP63 expressing cells started decreasing in cell area after about 1 min of photo-activation and reached a minimum of roughly 40% cell area decrease at 7 min.
source: The opposite effect was observed for OptoP63 expressing cells, they started decreasing in cell area after about 1 min of photo-activation and reached a minimum of roughly 40% cell area decrease at 7 min.
evidence: This is supported by cell area measurements over time shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After 7 min of photo-activation, OptoP63 expressing cells already recovered and increased in size, even though they were still photo-activated.
source: After this time point the OptoP63 expressing cells already recovered and increased in size, even though they were still photo-activated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by cell area measurements over time shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The cell area change of subconfluent cells upon activation and the vascular barrier strength upon activation showed a correlation.
source: To investigate if the cell size, specifically cell-cell overlap in a monolayer, plays a role in the observed barrier strength increase, the time scale of changes in cell area and resistance were compared. To this end, the cell area change of subconfluent cells, upon activation (Figure 4B), and the vascular barrier strength upon activation (Figure 2B) were compared and showed a correlation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.
